questions.stem: What is the difference between weathering and erosion?
options: Weathering breaks rock down in place; erosion carries the pieces away
Erosion breaks rock down in place; weathering carries the pieces away
Weathering happens only in deserts; erosion happens only along coasts
Weathering is caused by people; erosion is caused only by natural forces
questions.explanation: Weathering is the breaking down of rock where it sits, by temperature changes, water, ice, salt or chemical reactions. Erosion is the removal and transport of that broken material by water, wind, waves or ice. The two are easy to swap, so remember that erosion involves movement.

questions.stem: Which type of rock forms when molten magma or lava cools and hardens?
options: Metamorphic rock
Sandstone
Igneous rock
Sedimentary rock
questions.explanation: Igneous rocks such as granite and basalt form from cooled magma or lava. Sedimentary rocks such as sandstone form from layers of sediment pressed together, and metamorphic rocks form when existing rock is changed by heat and pressure. Hard igneous rock often resists erosion and stands out as hills or headlands.

questions.stem: What is the Pacific Ring of Fire?
options: A line of coral reefs heated by warm currents in the western Pacific
A band of hot deserts found at about 30° north and south of the equator
A belt of frequent earthquakes and volcanoes around the Pacific Ocean
A chain of bushfire-prone forests along the Pacific coast of America
questions.explanation: The Ring of Fire follows the edges of the Pacific plate and its neighbours, where plates collide, slide under each other or grind past each other. Japan, Indonesia, New Zealand and the west coast of the Americas all lie on it. Most of the world's active volcanoes and strongest earthquakes occur there.

questions.stem: K'gari (formerly Fraser Island) in Queensland is the world's largest:
options: Volcanic island
River delta
Sand island
Coral island
questions.explanation: K'gari is built almost entirely of sand carried north along the coast by waves and currents and piled up into huge dunes over hundreds of thousands of years. It is World Heritage listed for these dunes, its freshwater lakes and its rainforest growing on sand. Coral islands, such as those on the Great Barrier Reef, are much smaller.

questions.stem: In deserts, rock surfaces heat up strongly by day and cool at night, so thin outer layers crack and peel off. What is this process called?
options: Oxidation
Deposition
Carbonation
Exfoliation
questions.explanation: Exfoliation, sometimes called onion-skin weathering, is a type of physical weathering caused by repeated heating and cooling. Oxidation and carbonation are chemical weathering, where the minerals in the rock are changed by reactions with oxygen or acidic water. Deposition is the dropping of sediment, not the breaking of rock.

questions.stem: What is land reclamation, as used to create new land in Singapore and Tokyo Bay?
options: Cutting terraces into steep hillsides so that rice can be grown
Filling in shallow sea with sand and rock to make new land
Replanting cleared farmland so that it returns to native forest
Cleaning up polluted soil at old factory and mine sites
questions.explanation: Reclamation creates new dry land by filling shallow coastal water, and Singapore has enlarged its land area by about a quarter this way since the 1960s. It changes coastlines and can damage marine habitats, and the sand often has to be brought from other countries. Cleaning up polluted soil is called remediation, a different process.

questions.stem: What does World Heritage listing of a landscape, such as the Greater Blue Mountains, mean?
options: It is handed over to the United Nations, which then manages it and charges entry fees
It is closed to visitors so that the landforms and plants are left completely untouched
It may be mined or developed only by companies chosen through the United Nations
It is recognised as globally outstanding, and Australia has committed to protecting it
questions.explanation: World Heritage sites are places judged to have outstanding universal value, and the country where they are found agrees to protect them under the World Heritage Convention. Australia keeps ownership and management of its sites, such as the Blue Mountains, Uluru–Kata Tjuta and K'gari. Listing usually increases tourism rather than closing a site.

questions.stem: The Twelve Apostles in Victoria are limestone stacks. Which sequence of wave erosion forms a stack from a headland?
options: Spit, then cave, then stack
Cave, then arch, then stack
Stack, then arch, then cave
Arch, then cave, then stack
questions.explanation: Waves attack weaknesses in a headland and hollow out caves; when caves on both sides meet, an arch forms; when the arch roof collapses, the seaward pillar is left as a stack. The stacks keep eroding, which is why several of the Twelve Apostles have collapsed. A spit is a depositional landform, made by sand being dropped rather than rock being worn away.

questions.stem: The MacDonnell Ranges near Alice Springs are long, parallel ridges. What mainly formed them?
options: Rock layers folded and pushed up by tectonic forces, then eroded
A row of volcanoes that erupted along a crack in the Earth's crust
Huge sand dunes that were piled up by wind and then hardened into rock
Glaciers that carved deep valleys between the ridges during an ice age
questions.explanation: Hundreds of millions of years ago, tectonic forces squeezed and folded sedimentary rock layers into high mountains. Erosion has since worn them down, leaving the hardest layers as long ridges cut by gaps and gorges such as Standley Chasm. The ranges are not volcanic: their ridges are folded layers of sandstone and quartzite, not lava.

questions.stem: Why are the Himalayas still slowly rising today?
options: Volcanoes beneath the range keep adding new lava to the peaks
Rivers keep depositing sediment on top of the highest mountains
Melting glaciers make the rock lighter so that it floats upwards
The Indian plate is still pushing into the Eurasian plate
questions.explanation: The Himalayas formed where two continental plates collide: the Indian plate moves north into the Eurasian plate and the crust crumples and is pushed up. Because the collision is still happening, the mountains are still rising by a few millimetres a year. There are no active volcanoes in the Himalayas, because continental plates are too light to sink deep and melt the way ocean plates do.

questions.stem: Why did the huge earthquake off Sumatra in December 2004 cause a tsunami across the Indian Ocean?
options: Strong winds from a cyclone piled water against the coast of Sumatra
The earthquake triggered an unusually high tide caused by the Moon
A volcano on land erupted and sent hot ash and gas into the ocean
The sea floor suddenly moved, pushing a vast volume of water upwards
questions.explanation: The earthquake happened where one plate slides under another, and a long section of sea floor was suddenly pushed up, lifting the whole column of water above it. That water spread outwards as tsunami waves that reached Indonesia, Thailand, Sri Lanka, India and East Africa. A wave pushed ashore by cyclone winds is a storm surge, not a tsunami.

questions.stem: What triggered the 1997 Thredbo landslide in the New South Wales alpine region?
options: An earthquake on a nearby fault shook loose the rock on the steep slopes
A heavy snowfall slid off the mountain and buried the ski lodges below
A long drought dried the soil until it cracked and slid down the hill
Water from a leaking pipe soaked an unstable slope above the ski lodges
questions.explanation: The coroner found that a leaking water main had saturated the loose fill built up beside the Alpine Way road, until the slope gave way and destroyed two lodges, killing 18 people. It shows how human changes to a slope can turn a natural process into a disaster. A slide of snow is an avalanche, a different hazard.

questions.stem: Anangu, the Traditional Owners of Uluru, asked visitors not to climb the rock, and the climb was closed in 2019. What is their main reason?
options: The climb was damaging a rare plant that grows only on the summit
All World Heritage sites in Australia had to close their summit tracks
The climb follows a sacred ancestral route in Tjukurpa, Anangu law
The rock had become unstable and was likely to collapse onto walkers
questions.explanation: For Anangu, Uluru is a living cultural landscape, and the climb follows the route taken by ancestral Mala men, which is sacred under Tjukurpa, the foundation of Anangu law and life. Anangu also felt responsible for the safety of visitors, as people had died on the climb. The rock was not about to collapse, and no general rule closed World Heritage summits.

questions.stem: Caves such as those at Jenolan in New South Wales form when slightly acidic rainwater seeps through limestone. Which process is this?
options: Deposition, as water drops sediment carried from the surface
Abrasion, as fast rivers grind sand against the cave walls
Chemical weathering, as the acidic water dissolves the rock
Physical weathering, as ice wedges the rock apart in cracks
questions.explanation: Rainwater absorbs carbon dioxide, making a weak acid that slowly dissolves limestone along cracks, which over long periods hollows out caves. Because the minerals of the rock are changed, this is chemical weathering, often called carbonation or solution. Frost wedging is physical weathering, which breaks rock without changing its minerals.

questions.stem: A city lies on an active fault, and earthquakes there cannot be predicted to the day. Which strategy would most reduce deaths from a future earthquake?
options: Waiting for scientists to forecast the exact day of the quake
Building codes that make structures able to withstand shaking
Evacuating the whole city whenever a small tremor is felt
Building a sea wall to protect the city's main business area
questions.explanation: Most earthquake deaths are caused by buildings collapsing, so designing and strengthening buildings to flex without falling saves the most lives, as in Japan and New Zealand. Small tremors are common and rarely lead to a big quake, so evacuating each time would be unworkable. Scientists can map where quakes are likely, but not the exact day.

questions.stem: On a coast where bands of hard and soft rock meet the sea, why do headlands and bays form?
options: Hard rock wears away faster to form bays, leaving soft rock jutting out
Waves deposit sand on the hard rock until it builds outwards into headlands
The tide rises higher over soft rock, which floods it to make the bays
Soft rock wears away faster to form bays, leaving hard rock jutting out
questions.explanation: Waves erode soft rock such as clay more quickly than hard rock such as granite, so the coast is cut back into bays where the soft rock is, while the hard rock is left standing out as headlands. This is called differential erosion. Headlands are made of resistant rock, not built up from deposited sand.

questions.stem: Scientists now measure large earthquakes on the moment magnitude scale. About how much more energy does a magnitude 7 earthquake release than a magnitude 6?
options: About 2 times as much
About 100 times as much
About 32 times as much
About 10 times as much
questions.explanation: Each step of one on the magnitude scale means roughly 32 times more energy released, so a magnitude 7 releases about 1000 times the energy of a magnitude 5. The figure of 10 times is a common mix-up: it describes how much bigger the ground shaking recorded on a seismograph is, not the energy. This is why a small increase in magnitude means a much more destructive quake.

questions.stem: The Three Gorges Dam on the Yangtze River traps most of the sediment the river used to carry. What is a likely effect further downstream?
options: More sediment reaches the delta, so it grows much faster out to sea
The river carries more mud, so its channel fills up and floods more
The river stops flowing in summer because the dam holds all its water
Less sediment reaches the delta, so parts of the coast erode
questions.explanation: When a reservoir slows the river, sediment settles behind the dam instead of travelling to the river mouth. Without this supply, the delta and nearby coast are no longer built up and can be eroded by waves, and the riverbed below the dam can be scoured. The dam still releases water all year, generating hydro-electricity.

questions.stem: In 2011 the Tōhoku tsunami overtopped sea walls in many Japanese towns. What is the main lesson for managing tsunami risk?
options: Only buildings in the capital city need protecting, because that is where most people live
Defences can be exceeded, so warnings, drills and routes to high ground are also needed
Sea walls are useless, so all of them should be removed and replaced by wide beaches
Tsunamis can now be forecast days ahead, so no extra defences are needed on the coast
questions.explanation: The waves in 2011 were higher than many walls had been built for, and lives were saved where people knew to move quickly to high ground after the warning. Good hazard management combines engineering, early warning systems, evacuation drills and land-use zoning. Sea walls still reduce damage from smaller tsunamis, so removing them would increase risk.
